title: Jacob's disguise (Genesis 27)
hook: goat skins on his arms, Jacob steals his blind father's blessing

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birthright, the future traded for a bowl of red stew, and your line was not for a bowl of stew. Did you stop and ask what you were trading? Day three hundred sixty-one.

Isaac is old now, and his eyes are so dim he can't see. He calls in Esau, his favorite, and says: take your bow, hunt me some game, cook it the way I love it, and I'll give you my blessing before I die. In this story, a father's blessing is more than kind words. Once it is spoken, it can't be taken back. Rebekah is listening at the tent. She loves Jacob. And the moment Esau leaves for the field, she calls her younger son and tells him: go to the flock, bring me two young goats. We're going to make your father's favorite meal. And you're going to wear it.
screen: `AN OLD MAN WHO CAN'T SEE.` → `A BLESSING CAN'T BE TAKEN BACK.` → `REBEKAH IS LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Jacob's worry isn't whether it's wrong. It's whether it'll work. My brother is hairy, he says, and I'm smooth. What if my father touches me? So Rebekah dresses him in Esau's best clothes, so he'll smell of the field, and ties goat skins on his hands and the smooth of his neck. Jacob walks in with the meal. My father. Here I am; who are you, my son? And Jacob lies: I am Esau thy firstborn. Isaac is suspicious. How did you find it so quickly? Jacob even brings God into it: "Because the LORD thy God brought it to me." So Isaac says, come near, let me feel you. He runs his hands over the goat skins, and says, in the King James Bible: "The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau." He hears it. But the hands win, and the smell of the field, and he gives the blessing. Then Esau walks in with the real meal, and Isaac trembles, and Esau cries out with a great and bitter cry: "Bless me, even me also, O my father." And: is not he rightly named Jacob? His name, Ya'akov, sounds like heel, and like a word for one who grabs, who supplants. He's done it twice now. The text never praises the trick, and it shows the cost. Jacob has to run for his life, and Rebekah never sees her favorite son again in the story. Some readers, Jewish and Christian, see the promise going on through this grasping, frightened man. Not because of the lie, they say. In spite of it. Tomorrow, on the run, he has to sleep on a stone.
screen: `WILL IT WORK? NOT IS IT WRONG.` · `GOAT SKINS AND ESAU'S CLOTHES.` · `I AM ESAU THY FIRSTBORN.` · `A GREAT AND BITTER CRY.` · then, large: `THE VOICE IS JACOB'S VOICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: own one small deception. Settle, and breathe. Goat skins come in modern sizes. A little lie to get out of something. A version of yourself you put on for a boss, a parent, a date. A favor you took that was meant for someone else. Let one come to mind, a small one. Don't excuse it, and don't drown in it. Just name it honestly to yourself: that voice was mine. If you pray, you can bring it to God. After the bell, think whether there's one thing to set right. The bell holds the time.
Jacob's disguise. Goat skins on his arms and his brother's clothes, to steal his blind father's blessing, and a voice that gave him away.
Your line: the voice is jacob's. Today, take off one small disguise: tell the plain truth about one thing you've been dressing up. Day three hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Many Christians practice regular confession, privately, with a pastor, or in the sacrament of reconciliation, naming specific wrongs, and Jacob's story is often preached as a sign that God works through flawed people without approving their wrongs.

original.note: Hebrew: Jacob, a name that sounds like heel and like a word for one who supplants.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jacob cleverly got the blessing he deserved.
what it means: a son in disguise lies to his blind father, and the family breaks; the promise goes on in spite of the lie.
what a scholar hears: Ya'akov, heel and supplanter, named for grabbing twice; Isaac's line about the voice is the story's crack of truth.

notes: 'Rebekah never sees her favorite son again in the story': Genesis does not record a reunion; her death is not narrated (her burial is mentioned in 49:31). Confirm.
Ya'akov sounds like 'heel' (akev) and is explained by Esau as 'supplanted' (27:36). Confirm.
The power of a spoken blessing in the ancient world: 'believed to carry real power, and couldn't be taken back' (27:33, 37). Confirm.
'Christians and Jews have long noticed that God's promise still goes on through this grasping, frightened man': brief, unranked. Confirm.
I am Esau thy firstborn (27:19) is paraphrased-in-voice without quotation marks. Confirm.

Reviewer fix: myth reveal had "my brother is hairy, and I'm smooth" in quotation marks, which is not KJV wording (27:11: 'Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man'); now plain paraphrase. 'The text doesn't approve' softened to 'never praises the trick, and it shows the cost': readers differ here, and some Jewish and Christian interpreters defend Rebekah and Jacob in light of the oracle that the elder shall serve the younger (25:23). Keeper: confirm the lesson's moral framing is fair to those readings.
